overview: Section A is the base of the whole CIA program. It covers why internal auditing exists, where its authority comes from, what the charter must say, the two kinds of service (assurance and advisory), what threatens the function's independence, and where internal audit sits in the Three Lines Model. It carries the most weight in Part 1, and Parts 2 and 3 build on its rules.
analogy: Think of a building inspector hired by a city council, not by the builders. The council's written order says what the inspector may enter and inspect (the mandate, kept in the charter). The inspector tests the work against the building code and reports what was found (assurance), and may answer a builder's questions about a planned design (advice), but never pours the concrete or signs the builder's plans. If builders could set the inspector's budget, lock doors or choose what gets inspected, nobody could trust the reports. That is why the inspector answers to the council.

topics.overview: Domain I of the Global Internal Audit Standards states in a few lines why internal auditing exists and when it works best. This topic covers what the function gives the organization, what it improves, and the three conditions for effectiveness.
can_do: Describe what internal auditing provides, to whom, and to what end
List the five things internal auditing enhances in an organization
Explain the three conditions under which internal auditing works best
Tell internal audit's purpose apart from management's job of managing risk and running controls

subtopics.name: The Purpose Statement
subtopics.definition: The Purpose of Internal Auditing is the Standards' short statement of why the profession exists: to make an organization better at creating, protecting and sustaining value.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Every other rule in the Standards serves this purpose. If you know who internal audit serves and what it gives them, you can rule out answers that turn the auditor into a manager or a fraud detective.
how_it_works: Internal auditing serves two audiences inside the organization: the board and management.
It gives them four things: assurance, advice, insight and foresight.
Three qualities describe that work: independent, risk-based and objective.

The statement lists five gains: achieving objectives; stronger governance, risk management and control processes; better decisions and oversight; reputation and credibility; and serving the public interest.
Its effects reach beyond the organization, which is why the Standards are written with the public interest in mind.
Management, not internal audit, manages risk and runs controls. Internal audit assesses and advises.
subtopics.example: Kwame joins the internal audit team of a regional water utility in Ghana. A plant manager asks whether Kwame is there to find fraud and fix weak controls. Kwame explains that the team gives the board and management an independent view of how well risks are managed and controlled, plus advice, and that fixing controls stays with the plant's management.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Internal auditing strengthens the organization by giving the board and management independent, risk-based, objective assurance, advice, insight and foresight. It never manages risk, runs controls or makes management's decisions.

exam_traps.trap: The purpose of internal auditing is to manage the organization's risks and catch fraud.
exam_traps.why: Those are management's jobs. Internal audit gives assurance and advice on how well governance, risk management and control work. Considering fraud risk is part of that work, not its purpose.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit works for management only.
exam_traps.why: The statement names the board and management together, and the function is accountable directly to the board. Its work also helps the organization serve the public interest.

key_terms.definition: Domain I of the Standards: the short statement of why internal auditing exists and when it works best.
In plain terms, what the results mean and what may come next. The Standards name both and define neither further.
The well-being of society and its organizations, which the Standards are meant to serve.

subtopics.name: Conditions for Effective Internal Auditing
subtopics.definition: Conditions for effectiveness are the three things Domain I ties to internal auditing at its best: competent professionals following the Standards, independent positioning, and freedom from undue influence.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These conditions explain most of the governance rules that follow. A function that lacks skill, reports to the wrong level, or can be leaned on will produce reports nobody can rely on.
how_it_works: Condition one: the work is done by competent professionals who conform with the Global Internal Audit Standards.
Condition two: the internal audit function is positioned independently and answers directly to the board.
Condition three: nobody can pressure internal auditors into a view, and they commit to judging objectively.
The chief audit executive answers for the whole function's conformance. Every internal auditor answers for the standards that apply to their own work.
Conformance is expected. When a requirement truly cannot be met, the chief audit executive documents why and what was done instead.
subtopics.example: Aiko is asked to help set up internal audit at a family-owned logistics group in Japan. The owners want the team to report to the finance director and to skip the Standards to save time. Aiko explains that reports would carry little weight without skilled staff following the Standards, a direct line to the board, and freedom from pressure, and writes all three points into the proposal for the board.

review: Compare the function's actual reporting line with the charter and board minutes
Inspect training and certification records against the skills the plan needs
evidence: Quality assessment results on conformance with the Standards
Board minutes showing direct sessions with the chief audit executive
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive report gaps in skills, positioning or freedom from pressure to the board with proposed safeguards.
audit_focus.decides: The board decides how the function is positioned and supported

subtopics.isaca_rule: Internal auditing is most effective when three things hold together: competent people conforming with the Standards, a function positioned independently and directly accountable to the board, and auditors free from undue influence.

exam_traps.trap: Independent positioning and conformance are good practice that a small or busy function can drop.
exam_traps.why: Domain I names them as conditions for effectiveness, and conformance is expected of every function whatever its size. An unmet requirement is documented with the reason and the alternative.

exam_traps.trap: Independence and objectivity are the same condition.
exam_traps.why: The second condition is about where the function sits (independence). The third is about each auditor's unbiased mindset (objectivity). Exam answers treat them separately.

key_terms.definition: Meeting the requirements of the Standards. The chief audit executive answers for it across the function.
Pressure from management or others that could bend an auditor's judgment or findings.
The function answers to the board itself, not to the managers it reviews.

topics.topic_name: The mandate and who sets it
topics.overview: The mandate is what internal audit is allowed and expected to do. This topic covers what the mandate contains, where it comes from, how the chief audit executive helps set and refresh it, and what the board and senior management each do. It is also a CIA Challenge Exam topic.
can_do: Explain what a mandate contains and where it comes from
Explain what the chief audit executive supplies so that the mandate can be set, and when it is revisited
Tell the board's part from senior management's part in setting and supporting the mandate
Explain what the chief audit executive does when the board or senior management will not provide an essential condition

subtopics.name: The Internal Audit Mandate
subtopics.definition: The internal audit mandate is the function's authority, role and responsibilities, given by the board, by laws and regulations, or by both.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The mandate is the source of the function's power to audit any part of the organization. Without it, a manager could refuse access or argue that an area is off limits.
how_it_works: Authority comes from the direct reporting line to the board. It brings unrestricted access to the board and to records, people and property.
Role: mainly to deliver internal audit services. Roles such as risk management or compliance may be added to the chief audit executive's duties and then need safeguards.
Responsibilities are what the function answers for: performing services, communicating, following laws and policies, and conforming with the Standards.
Scope says how much of the organization is covered and which services are offered, such as assurance alone, or both assurance and advice.
The mandate comes from the board, from law or regulation (common in the public sector), or both, and is recorded in the charter.
subtopics.example: Thandiwe, a new internal auditor at a South African insurer, is refused claims files by a manager who says internal audit has no right to customer data. Thandiwe checks the board-approved charter: the mandate gives the function unrestricted access to the records its work needs. Thandiwe shows the manager the clause and, when access is still refused, reports the restriction to the engagement supervisor.

review: Trace the function's authority, role and responsibilities to the approved charter
Compare the charter's scope with any mandate set by law or regulation
evidence: Minutes of the board meeting that adopted the mandate
Text of any statute or regulation prescribing internal audit's duties
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management and the board resolve any gap between the charter's scope and what the law prescribes.
audit_focus.decides: The board, or lawmakers where the mandate is legal

subtopics.isaca_rule: The mandate is authority, role and responsibilities. It comes from the board, from law, or both, and it lives in the charter. The chief audit executive informs and documents but does not grant it.

exam_traps.trap: The chief audit executive sets the mandate, because the chief audit executive writes the charter.
exam_traps.why: Drafting is not granting. The chief audit executive supplies information and documents the mandate. The board establishes and approves it, unless law or regulation prescribes it.

exam_traps.trap: A mandate must always come from the board.
exam_traps.why: It may be prescribed wholly or partly by laws or regulations, as often happens in the public sector. Then the charter must include those legal requirements.

key_terms.definition: The power to do the work, created by the direct line to the board. It carries unrestricted access.
Freedom to reach the data, records, people and property the work needs.

subtopics.name: The Chief Audit Executive's Part in Setting the Mandate
subtopics.definition: The chief audit executive's part in the mandate is to supply the information the board and senior management need, record the result in the charter, and keep it current.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A board can only grant a sensible mandate if it understands what internal audit can do and what other assurance providers already cover. The chief audit executive is the person who knows.
how_it_works: The chief audit executive must give the board and senior management the information needed to establish the mandate, such as what the Standards and the law expect.
Before scope is set, the chief audit executive must work out with the other assurance providers, inside and outside the organization, who covers what.
The mandate must be written into the charter, or referenced there, by the chief audit executive.
Periodically, the chief audit executive must assess whether changed circumstances call for a fresh discussion of the mandate with the board and senior management.
Typical triggers: changed Standards, an acquisition or reorganization, new board members or senior managers, new strategy or risks, new laws. A formal check should happen at least yearly.
subtopics.example: Mariana becomes chief audit executive of a Brazilian retailer just after it buys an online payments company. Mariana briefs the board and senior management on what the Standards expect, maps what compliance and the external auditor already cover, and proposes adding the payments business to the scope. After the discussion, Mariana updates the draft charter and submits it to the board.

review: Trace each charter change to a documented discussion with the board
Compare the date of the last mandate review with major organizational changes
evidence: Dated record of the yearly check on whether the mandate still fits
Briefing papers on leading practices and on who else gives assurance
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive table the mandate for discussion after any acquisition, restructuring or change of leadership.
audit_focus.decides: The board, after weighing executives' views

subtopics.isaca_rule: The chief audit executive informs, coordinates, documents and revisits. When circumstances change, the chief audit executive raises the mandate with the board and senior management; the board decides whether it changes.

exam_traps.trap: Once the board approves the charter, the mandate is settled and need not be discussed again.
exam_traps.why: The chief audit executive must periodically assess whether circumstances justify a new discussion. The considerations suggest a formal look at least once a year.

key_terms.definition: Any internal or external party that gives assurance, such as compliance, risk management or the external auditor.
A practice the Standards' considerations describe as preferred. It is advice, not a requirement.
The chief audit executive's periodic check that authority, role and responsibilities still fit the function's strategy and objectives.

subtopics.name: What the Board and Senior Management Each Do
subtopics.definition: Board and senior management roles in the mandate are split: the board discusses and approves, while senior management gives input and supports it across the organization.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Exam questions often swap these two parties. Board approval keeps internal audit independent of the managers it reviews; management's support makes the mandate work day to day.
how_it_works: The board discusses the right authority, role and responsibilities with the chief audit executive and senior management.
The board approves the internal audit charter, which holds the mandate and the scope and types of services.
Senior management joins the discussion and gives input on expectations the board should consider.
Senior management supports the mandate across the organization and promotes the authority given to the function.
The board also approves the plan, budget and resource plan, and sets a reporting level that lets the function fulfill the mandate.
Both work together so the function can reach the data, records, people and property it needs.

rows.label: Mandate
cells: Supplies information and documents it in the charter

rows.label: Plan, budget, resource plan
cells: Discusses them; works with the board on resources

rows.label: Access to records and people
cells: Works with senior management to enable it
Works with the board and other managers to enable it

rows.label: Recognition of the function
cells: Provides the information needed to promote it

subtopics.example: At a Canadian credit union, the chief executive officer tells Priya, an internal auditor, that the executive team has 'signed off' a narrower audit scope that leaves out lending. Priya knows senior management gives input but does not approve the charter or its scope. Priya reports the conversation to the chief audit executive, who raises the proposed change with the board.

review: Inspect board minutes for the vote approving the charter and its scope
Compare who signed the charter with who the Standards say approves it
evidence: Signed, dated charter showing the approving body
Correspondence recording what executives asked internal audit to cover
audit_focus.recommend: Have management route every request to narrow or widen audit coverage through the board's approval process.
audit_focus.decides: The board votes; executives are consulted beforehand

subtopics.isaca_rule: The board approves; senior management gives input and support. An answer that has senior management approving the charter, the plan or the budget, alone or jointly with the board, describes the older rule and is wrong.

exam_traps.trap: The charter is approved by senior management and the board together.
exam_traps.why: Under the 2024 Standards the chief audit executive discusses the charter with both, and the board alone approves it. Joint approval is the pre-2024 rule.

exam_traps.trap: Senior management has no part in the mandate, because involving it would harm independence.
exam_traps.why: Senior management's input is an essential condition, and its support makes the mandate effective. Input is not approval.

key_terms.definition: What the Standards mean by the board: for example a board of directors, or an audit committee acting for it.
To speak up for and back the internal audit function so it can meet its purpose.
The chief audit executive's plan for the people, money and technology the audit plan needs.

subtopics.memory_aid: The chief audit executive drafts, both discuss, the board approves, senior management supports.

subtopics.name: Essential Conditions and Disagreements
subtopics.definition: Essential conditions are the board and senior management activities that Domain III says internal audit needs to fulfill its purpose; they are not requirements on the board.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The Standards bind internal auditors, not directors. A chief audit executive cannot order a board to act; the duty is to discuss, explain and document.
how_it_works: The chief audit executive must discuss Domain III with the board and senior management, including the effect on internal audit if their support is missing.
If either disagrees with a condition, the chief audit executive must show, with examples, how its absence may harm the function or its conformance.
The chief audit executive should also suggest alternatives that could give the same result.
If all agree a condition is not needed, the chief audit executive must document the reasons and the alternative conditions that compensate.
If the chief audit executive rejects their reasons, the function may be unable to conform. The reasons should be documented, shared and kept for the external assessor.
subtopics.example: Joon-ho is chief audit executive of a Korean manufacturer whose board chair refuses private sessions without the chief executive officer. Joon-ho explains, with examples, how sensitive matters about senior management could go unreported, and offers an alternative: a standing slot with the audit committee chair alone. The board accepts. Joon-ho documents the reasons and the alternative condition for the next external quality assessment.

review: Compare each Domain III essential condition with what the board actually does
Inspect the file kept for the external assessor on conditions not provided
evidence: Agenda and minutes of the meeting where Domain III was presented
Signed memo listing each waived condition and its substitute
audit_focus.recommend: Have the board and senior management confirm in writing which conditions they provide and which substitutes apply.
audit_focus.decides: The board and senior management decide whether to provide the condition

subtopics.isaca_rule: Board duties are essential conditions, not rules the chief audit executive can enforce. When one is missing: discuss, show the impact with examples, propose alternatives and document the outcome.

exam_traps.trap: The Standards require the board to approve the charter, so a board that refuses is violating the Standards.
exam_traps.why: The Standards place requirements on internal auditors. Board and senior management duties are essential conditions; the chief audit executive's requirement is to discuss them and document the outcome.

exam_traps.trap: If the board rejects a condition, the chief audit executive should accept it quietly and carry on.
exam_traps.why: The chief audit executive must explain the impact with examples and document the outcome. Without an adequate alternative, the function may be unable to conform.

key_terms.definition: Board and senior management activities listed in each Domain III standard as necessary for an effective internal audit function.
A substitute arrangement that compensates for an absent essential condition, documented with the reasons.

topics.overview: The internal audit charter is the formal document that holds the mandate. This topic covers the minimum content the Standards require, why the chief audit executive discusses the draft with the board and senior management, and why the board must be the one to approve it.
can_do: Recognize the four items every charter must contain
Tell required charter content from optional topics and from items that are not charter content
Explain why the draft goes to both the board and senior management for discussion
Recognize who approves the charter and why that matters for independence

subtopics.name: Required Charter Content
subtopics.definition: The internal audit charter is the formal document that records the function's mandate, position, reporting lines, scope and types of service.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The charter is the first place to look when someone questions internal audit's right to act. A missing element, such as the reporting line, leaves the function exposed.
how_it_works: Minimum content one: the Purpose of Internal Auditing.
Minimum content two: a commitment to adhere to the Global Internal Audit Standards.
Minimum content three: the mandate, with scope, types of services, and what the board expects of management in supporting the function.
Minimum content four: the function's organizational position and reporting relationships.
Also required where they apply: the mandate's legal requirements, and any ongoing role the chief audit executive holds beyond internal auditing, with its safeguards.
Other topics should be considered: handling of impairments, unrestricted access, communication with the board, the audit process, quality assessments, and how budgets are approved.
subtopics.example: Farid, an internal auditor at a hospital group in the United Arab Emirates, reads the draft charter before it goes to the board. It states the purpose, the mandate and the scope, but says nothing about following the Standards or about where the function reports. Farid lists the two missing required items and sends the draft back to the chief audit executive.

review: Compare the charter against the four minimum items in Standard 6.2
Inspect whether nonaudit roles and their safeguards are written into the charter
evidence: Current charter with the date the board approved it
Checklist mapping charter sections to the required content
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive add the absent sections and bring the revised text to the next board meeting.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the charter's content

subtopics.isaca_rule: A charter states at least four things: the Purpose of Internal Auditing, the commitment to the Standards, the mandate with scope and services, and the organizational position and reporting relationships. The internal audit plan and the budget are not on the list.

exam_traps.trap: The charter must contain the internal audit plan and the budget.
exam_traps.why: Neither is required charter content. The charter may describe how budgets are approved, but the plan and the budget are separate items the board approves.

exam_traps.trap: The charter and the mandate are the same thing.
exam_traps.why: The mandate is the authority, role and responsibilities. The charter is the document that holds it, along with the purpose, the commitment to the Standards and the reporting relationships.

key_terms.definition: Where the function sits in the structure, set by the board so it can work without interference.
The chief audit executive's lines: directly to the board, and administratively to a member of management.
The kinds of work the function offers, such as assurance and advice.

subtopics.memory_aid: Purpose, Standards, mandate, position: the four charter musts.

subtopics.name: Discussing the Charter with the Board and Senior Management
subtopics.definition: Discussing the charter means the chief audit executive takes the proposed text to the board and senior management to confirm it matches what they understand and expect.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A charter that management has never seen will be resisted in practice, and one the board does not understand may not be approved. Discussion builds the shared understanding that later makes access and cooperation easier.
how_it_works: The chief audit executive develops the charter and keeps it up to date.
Before approval, the proposed charter must be discussed with both the board and senior management.
The aim is to confirm the wording matches what both groups understand and expect of internal audit.
The board is expected to raise other topics the charter should cover to make the function effective.
Senior management is expected to tell the board and the chief audit executive what management expects, so it can be considered for inclusion.
Typically the final draft is presented at a board meeting, discussed there and approved.
subtopics.example: Ngozi, chief audit executive of a Nigerian telecom, drafts a charter that adds advisory services. Before the board meeting, Ngozi walks the chief executive officer and the finance director through the draft and notes their expectations about notice before engagements. Ngozi then presents the final draft to the audit committee, explains management's input, and asks the board to approve it.

review: Trace the draft charter to recorded discussions with senior management and the board
Compare expectations raised in discussion with the final charter wording
evidence: Tracked-changes versions of the charter showing whose comments were adopted
Board papers that summarize executives' comments on the proposed text
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive record executives' comments on each draft and show the board how they were handled.
audit_focus.decides: The board votes on the final text

subtopics.isaca_rule: Discuss with both, approve by one. The chief audit executive discusses the proposed charter with the board and senior management so it reflects their expectations; then the board approves it.

exam_traps.trap: Discussing the draft with senior management compromises independence, so it should go straight to the board.
exam_traps.why: The Standards require the discussion with both. Hearing management's expectations does not hand management control; the board still decides and approves.

exam_traps.trap: Because senior management reviewed the charter, its sign-off completes the approval.
exam_traps.why: Discussion is not approval. Senior management communicates expectations; the approval belongs to the board.

key_terms.definition: The chief audit executive's draft, taken to the board and senior management for discussion before approval.
What senior management hopes internal audit will cover or how it will work; input the board may weigh.

subtopics.name: Board Approval and Keeping the Charter Current
subtopics.definition: Board approval of the charter is the act that gives the internal audit function its formal authority; the charter is then reviewed when circumstances change.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Authority granted by the board cannot be taken away by a manager who dislikes a finding. Approval by anyone lower would make internal audit depend on the people it audits.
how_it_works: The board approves the charter. The chief audit executive who drafted it does not, and neither does senior management.
Approval shows the board's support and fixes the reporting level the board has determined.
The board reviews the charter with the chief audit executive when things change, such as a new chief audit executive or a shift in the organization's risks.
The chief audit executive and the board should agree how often to review and reaffirm the charter. Periodic review is a leading practice.
Changes to the charter go back to the board for approval. Changes that may affect it are reported to the board and senior management.
subtopics.example: Tomasz joins internal audit at a Polish energy company and finds the charter was last approved six years ago, before the company entered renewable power and before the current chief audit executive arrived. Tomasz raises this with the chief audit executive, who reviews the charter, discusses updates with senior management and the board, and submits the revised charter for board approval.

review: Compare the charter's approval date with changes in leadership, strategy and risks
Inspect whether the agreed review frequency was kept
evidence: Minutes recording the vote on the charter and on each amendment
Calendar entry or policy fixing how often the charter is reaffirmed
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive schedule the next charter check now and tie it to leadership or strategy changes.
audit_focus.decides: The board votes on the original and on every amendment

subtopics.isaca_rule: Only the board approves the charter. Approval by the chief audit executive is self-approval; approval by senior management puts the function under the people it audits. Review the charter when the organization, its risks or the chief audit executive changes.

exam_traps.trap: The chief audit executive approves the charter, being accountable for the function.
exam_traps.why: The chief audit executive develops and maintains it. Authority has to come from above the function, so the board approves.

exam_traps.trap: A charter approved once stays valid until the Standards change.
exam_traps.why: The board reviews it with the chief audit executive when circumstances change, such as a new chief audit executive or new risks, and the two should agree a review frequency.

key_terms.definition: The board's formal decision to adopt the charter, usually recorded in meeting minutes with a date.
To confirm, after review, that the charter still lets the function meet its objectives.

topics.overview: Internal audit gives two kinds of service. Assurance is an objective assessment against criteria that raises confidence. Advisory work is advice with no assurance and no management responsibility. This topic covers both, the two levels of assurance, how advisory scope is agreed, and how to pick the right service.
can_do: Tell an assurance engagement from an advisory engagement in a scenario
Explain what decides whether assurance is limited or reasonable
Explain who settles what an advisory engagement covers, and who sets objectives and scope for assurance
Choose the service that fits a request and name the safeguards that apply

subtopics.name: Assurance Services
subtopics.definition: Assurance services are objective assessments in which internal auditors compare an activity with set criteria and state a conclusion that raises stakeholders' confidence in it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The board and senior management rely on assurance to know whether governance, risk management and control processes work. That reliance is only justified if the auditors, not the people being reviewed, shaped the work.
how_it_works: Assurance is a statement meant to raise confidence about governance, risk management and control processes, measured against established criteria.
Internal auditors compare the existing condition with the criteria. A gap is a potential finding.
The engagement ends in a conclusion on effectiveness, and it says so when processes are working well.
Objectives and scope are set mainly by the internal auditors, and the chief audit executive approves them.
Its main users are the board, senior managers and the managers of the area reviewed.
Examples in the Standards include engagements on compliance, on financial matters, on operations or performance, and on technology.
subtopics.example: The board of a Kenyan agricultural lender asks whether loan approvals follow the credit policy. Wanjiru, an internal auditor, sets the objectives and scope, uses the credit policy as criteria, tests a sample of approved loans, and compares what happened with what the policy requires. Wanjiru documents the gaps as potential findings and drafts a conclusion on whether the approval controls are effective.

review: Compare the condition found with the criteria agreed during planning
Trace each finding and the conclusion to evidence in the workpapers
evidence: Test results obtained directly by the internal auditors
Planning memo naming the yardstick chosen and why it is adequate
audit_focus.recommend: Have the management of the activity under review prepare action plans that address the root cause of each finding.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides and carries out the actions; the board oversees

subtopics.isaca_rule: Assurance means criteria, evidence and a conclusion. The internal auditors decide the objectives and scope, and the conclusion states whether processes are effective, including when they are.

exam_traps.trap: The manager of the audited area sets the scope of an assurance engagement.
exam_traps.why: Management's input is considered, but the internal auditors mainly set assurance objectives and scope and the chief audit executive approves them. Otherwise the reviewed party could steer the result.

exam_traps.trap: An assurance report only matters when it lists problems.
exam_traps.why: When no gap is found, the conclusion still gives assurance that the processes are effective. Reporting that things work is part of the service.

key_terms.definition: The yardstick for the engagement: what the activity should look like, taken from policy, law, contracts or good practice.
What the internal auditors actually found: the existing state of the activity.
The auditors' overall verdict on the engagement results, taken together.

subtopics.name: Limited and Reasonable Assurance
subtopics.definition: Limited and reasonable assurance are the two levels of assurance the Standards name; which one applies depends on what procedures were done, when, and how much.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Readers act on the level of confidence a report claims. Claiming more than the work supports misleads the board, so the words in the conclusion have to match the procedures behind it.
how_it_works: The Standards glossary says internal auditors may give limited or reasonable assurance, and ties the choice to the procedures performed.
Three features of the procedures matter: their nature (what kind), their timing (when, and for which period) and their extent (how much).
The Standards name the two levels and define neither. As the everyday words suggest, limited assurance rests on less work and gives less confidence than reasonable assurance.
Neither level is a guarantee. Assurance raises confidence; it does not promise that nothing is wrong, and auditors are not expected to be infallible.
A function's methodologies may use a rating scale to show whether reasonable assurance exists on control effectiveness.
subtopics.example: Camille, an internal auditor at a French university, is asked for a quick review of research grant spending. Time allows only interviews and a read of the procedures for one month, not testing of transactions across the year. Camille tells the engagement supervisor that this work supports only a limited level of assurance, and words the conclusion to say what was and was not tested.

review: Compare the level of assurance stated with the procedures in the work program
Inspect the conclusion for claims the evidence does not support
evidence: Work program listing each test, its sample size and the months covered
Final communication wording on what was and was not examined
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set out in the methodologies how conclusions state the level of assurance.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive approves the final communication

subtopics.isaca_rule: The level of assurance follows the work done. Match the conclusion to the nature, timing and extent of the procedures, and never claim more confidence than the evidence supports. Reasonable does not mean absolute.

exam_traps.trap: Reasonable assurance means the internal auditors guarantee there are no errors or fraud.
exam_traps.why: No level of assurance is absolute. Assurance increases confidence, and due professional care does not make auditors infallible.

exam_traps.trap: The level of assurance depends on how senior the requester is.
exam_traps.why: It depends on the procedures: what kind, when and how much. A board request does not turn a light review into reasonable assurance.

key_terms.definition: The kind of work done, such as interviews, inspection of records or direct testing.
When the work is done and which period it covers.
How much is examined, such as the size of a sample or a whole population.

subtopics.name: Advisory Services and How Their Scope Is Agreed
subtopics.definition: Advisory services are services in which internal auditors give advice to stakeholders without giving assurance and without taking on management responsibilities.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Advisory work lets internal audit help before problems occur. The risk is drifting from adviser to decision maker, which would damage objectivity and any later assurance over the same area.
how_it_works: Advisory work can begin with the internal auditors' own suggestion or with a request from the board, senior management or an activity's managers.
The nature and scope are agreed with the party requesting the service. Objectives and scope are typically set jointly.
The work program should be developed together with the stakeholders who asked for the service.
Depending on that agreement, a formal documented risk assessment, evaluation criteria and evidence-based findings may not be needed.
The other requirements still apply, including objectivity, competency, due professional care and the chief audit executive's approval of objectives and scope.
The Three Lines Model adds that the board should know what advisory work is under way.
subtopics.example: The procurement head of a Singapore shipping firm asks internal audit for advice on a draft supplier onboarding policy. Wei Ling, the internal auditor, agrees the scope with the procurement head: comment on control gaps, no testing, no sign-off. Wei Ling gets the chief audit executive's approval and gives written suggestions. Procurement chooses which to adopt, and Wei Ling records that the work gave advice, not assurance.

review: Compare the agreed advisory scope with the work actually performed
Inspect advisory files for decisions taken by internal auditors instead of management
evidence: Signed terms of the engagement, stating what is in and out
Sign-off sheet showing who authorized the engagement to start
audit_focus.recommend: Have the requesting management own every decision and record that internal audit's input was advice only.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides what to adopt from the advice

subtopics.isaca_rule: Advisory work is advice without assurance and without management responsibility. Its nature and scope are agreed with the requesting party, the Standards still apply unless a standard says otherwise, and management makes every decision.

exam_traps.trap: Advisory work is informal, so the Standards do not apply to it.
exam_traps.why: The Standards apply to assurance and advisory work alike, except where an individual standard says otherwise. Only specific items, such as a formal risk assessment or criteria, may be unnecessary.

exam_traps.trap: Because management asked for help, the auditor can make the design decision for them.
exam_traps.why: Advice stops short of deciding. Taking on management responsibility impairs objectivity and blocks credible assurance over that area later.

key_terms.definition: The board, senior management or activity management that asks for an advisory service and agrees its scope.
Deciding, approving, implementing or owning a process or control. It stays with management in every engagement.

subtopics.name: Choosing the Right Service
subtopics.definition: Choosing the service means deciding, from what the stakeholder needs and what the charter allows, whether an engagement should give assurance or advice.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Internal auditors must consider which type an engagement is, because expectations and requirements differ. A wrong label leaves the board believing it has assurance it never received.
how_it_works: Ask what is needed: confidence that something works against criteria (assurance), or input to improve or design something (advisory).
When no adequate criteria exist, the discussion may lead to advisory work that helps management develop them.
A request to swap a planned assurance engagement for advisory work is a conflicting demand that the chief audit executive reports to the board and senior management.
Assurance may follow advisory work in the same area only if the chief audit executive confirms objectivity is not impaired and staffs the engagement to manage it.
An auditor responsible for an activity in the previous 12 months may not give assurance on it, but may advise after disclosure to the requesting party.

rows.label: What is delivered
cells: A conclusion against criteria that raises confidence

rows.label: Risk assessment, criteria, findings
cells: May not be needed, depending on the agreement

rows.label: Topical Requirements
cells: Mandatory when the topic is in scope

subtopics.example: A logistics company in Mexico plans a new warehouse system. The operations director asks internal audit to 'audit' the design, but no approved requirements exist to test against and the director mainly wants ideas on controls. Diego, the internal auditor, concludes that advice fits better, explains that no assurance will be given, and notes that later assurance must be staffed to protect objectivity.

review: Compare each engagement's label with what was actually delivered
Trace assurance engagements that followed advisory work to the objectivity confirmation
evidence: Planning records stating which of the two services is intended
Staffing sheet showing who advised earlier and who now tests
audit_focus.recommend: Have the board see every proposal to trade a planned audit for advice before the plan changes.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves significant changes to the internal audit plan

subtopics.isaca_rule: Confidence against criteria is assurance; input on something being built or improved is advisory. Assurance can follow advice only when the chief audit executive confirms no impairment, and never from someone responsible for the work in the past 12 months.

exam_traps.trap: Once internal audit has advised on an area, it can never audit that area.
exam_traps.why: It can, if the chief audit executive confirms the earlier advice does not impair objectivity and staffs the engagement accordingly.

exam_traps.trap: A former manager of the area cannot even give advice on it.
exam_traps.why: The 12-month presumption applies to assurance. Advice on a former responsibility is allowed after disclosing the possible impairment to the requesting party before accepting.

key_terms.definition: Competing requests for internal audit's time; the chief audit executive reports them to the board and senior management.
Objectivity is presumed impaired for assurance on an activity the auditor was responsible for in the previous 12 months.

subtopics.memory_aid: Confidence against criteria: assurance. Help while building: advisory.

topics.overview: Assurance engagements come in several kinds, named for what they examine. This topic describes each kind the syllabus lists, what it looks at and why, so you can match a scenario to the right engagement.
can_do: Describe what each kind of assurance engagement examines
Tell an operational audit from a compliance audit and from a financial audit
Explain why access rights in a contract matter for work on third parties
Describe what an audit of culture and an audit of management reporting look at

subtopics.name: Risk and Control Assessments
subtopics.definition: A risk and control assessment is an assurance engagement that asks whether the controls over an activity's significant risks are well designed and working.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Almost every assurance engagement has this logic at its core: objective, risk, control. Knowing it lets you place the other engagement types as variations with a narrower focus.
how_it_works: The auditors first understand the activity's objectives, then identify the risks that could stop those objectives being met.
Risks are ranked by significance, usually by impact and likelihood, and the most significant are reviewed first.
For the most significant risks, assessing control design first helps decide which controls are worth testing for operation.
Controls tested typically deal with authority and responsibility, compliance, reliable reporting, efficient use of resources and safeguarding of assets.
A risk and control matrix may be used to link objectives, risks and controls.
Fraud risks are considered in every engagement risk assessment.
subtopics.example: Lucía, an internal auditor at a pharmacy chain in Chile, reviews controlled-drug inventory. Lucía confirms the objective (drugs are accounted for), lists the risks (theft, miscounts), and maps the controls (locked storage, dual counts). The dual count looks well designed, so Lucía tests whether two people really sign each count. Lucía records the results in a risk and control matrix and drafts the findings.

review: Walk the process to confirm how each key control is meant to work
Evaluate control design before sampling transactions to test operation
Compare the remaining risk with management's risk tolerance, where defined
evidence: Reperformance and inspection results the audit team produced itself
Process narrative or flowchart confirmed by the people who run it
audit_focus.recommend: Have process management redesign controls that cannot manage the risk and fix those that do not operate.
audit_focus.decides: Management chooses the risk response within the organization's risk appetite

subtopics.isaca_rule: Start from the activity's objectives, then the risks to them, then the controls. Judge design before operation. Management owns the risks and the controls; the auditors assess them.

exam_traps.trap: Test how the controls operate first; design can be looked at if time allows.
exam_traps.why: A badly designed control cannot manage the risk even if it runs perfectly. Assessing design first shows which controls are worth testing.

exam_traps.trap: The internal auditors decide which risks the activity should accept.
exam_traps.why: The auditors assess and report. Management decides how to respond to risks, within the appetite and tolerance the organization has set.

key_terms.definition: A working table that sets each objective beside its risks and the controls meant to manage them.
Whether a control, if it works as intended, is able to manage the risk.
Whether the control actually works as designed, consistently, over the period.

subtopics.name: Operational, Financial, Compliance, Performance and Quality Audits
subtopics.definition: Operational, financial and compliance audits are the classic assurance engagements; each tests one kind of objective: efficient operations, reliable financial information, or adherence to rules.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Exam scenarios describe what the auditors are checking and ask you to name the engagement. The quickest route is to ask which objective is being tested.
how_it_works: Each kind is named for the objective it tests. The steps of the engagement stay the same.
The Standards glossary gives engagements on compliance, financial matters, operations or performance, and technology as examples of assurance services.
Four risk areas run through them: reliable financial and operational information, effective and efficient operations, safeguarding of assets, and compliance with laws and regulations.
One engagement can combine kinds, for example an operational audit that also tests compliance with a safety regulation.
Internal audit's financial work serves the board and management. The external auditor's opinion on the financial statements serves outside stakeholders and sits outside the three lines.

types.meaning: Examines how effectively and efficiently an operation or program achieves its objectives.
Asks whether results match goals. In the public sector it often covers economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
Examines the reliability and integrity of financial information and the controls that produce it.
Checks adherence to the laws and regulations that apply to the organization.
In general terms, checks whether a product, service or process meets the quality requirements set for it.

subtopics.example: A Vietnamese garment maker asks internal audit to review its cutting department. Minh, the internal auditor, is told to find out why fabric waste is above target and whether machine time is well used. No law or policy is being tested, and no financial figures are being verified. Minh identifies the work as an operational audit and takes the department's own waste and output targets as criteria.

review: Identify the objective under test before choosing criteria and procedures
Compare actual results with the targets, rules or records that serve as criteria
evidence: Production, cost and quality data extracted by the audit team
The statute, license condition or internal rule being tested against
audit_focus.recommend: Have the management of the activity address the root cause of each gap between results and criteria.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the operation and decides how to improve it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Name the engagement by the objective tested: efficiency and effectiveness is operational, adherence to a rule is compliance, reliability of financial information is financial. Internal audit's financial work is not the external auditor's opinion.

exam_traps.trap: An audit that asks whether a process is efficient is a compliance audit, because the process has procedures.
exam_traps.why: Compliance audits test adherence to a rule. When the question is how well resources are used or goals are met, the engagement is operational or performance.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit's financial audit gives the opinion on the financial statements.
exam_traps.why: That opinion comes from the external auditor and serves outside parties. Internal audit gives the board and management assurance on financial information and its controls.

key_terms.definition: Following the rules that bind the organization: laws, regulations, contracts and its own policies.
An outside firm that gives an independent opinion, mainly on financial statements, for stakeholders outside the organization.

subtopics.name: Third-Party, Contract Compliance, IT Security and Privacy Audits
subtopics.definition: Third-party, contract compliance, IT security and privacy audits are assurance engagements over risks that sit with outside parties, information systems and personal data.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An organization stays accountable even when a supplier does the work or a system holds the data. These audits tell the board whether those exposures are governed and controlled.
how_it_works: A third-party audit looks at how the organization selects, contracts, onboards, monitors and exits its suppliers and other outside parties.
A contract compliance audit checks whether the terms of a contract are being met by the parties to it.
Access matters: without a right-to-audit clause, internal audit's ability to obtain or give assurance over a third party may be limited.
An IT security audit looks at how the organization governs, risk-manages and controls the protection of its systems and data.
A privacy audit checks how personal information is protected and whether privacy laws, regulations and policies are followed.
Where a Topical Requirement covers the subject, as for cybersecurity, it is the mandatory minimum baseline for assurance on that topic.
subtopics.example: A Philippine bank outsources card printing. Jun, an internal auditor, plans to visit the printer's site to test how card data is protected, but the contract has no right-to-audit clause and the printer declines. Jun reports the restriction to the engagement supervisor, asks for the printer's independent assurance report instead, and recommends adding audit rights at renewal.

review: Inspect key contracts for audit rights and for security and privacy terms
Compare the supplier's actual performance with the contract terms
Evaluate management's ongoing monitoring of high-risk third parties
evidence: Service-level and incident data for the supplier, obtained directly
Signed agreements with their security and data protection schedules
Complete list of third-party relationships ranked by risk
audit_focus.recommend: Have contract owners negotiate audit rights into high-risk agreements and review supplier performance on a set schedule.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the third-party relationship and its risks

subtopics.isaca_rule: Outsourcing moves the work, not the accountability. Internal audit assesses how management governs and controls third parties, systems and personal data, and needs agreed access to do so.

exam_traps.trap: A contract compliance audit can always go ahead, because internal audit has unrestricted access.
exam_traps.why: The charter grants access inside the organization. Access to a third party's records depends on the contract; without a right-to-audit clause, assurance may be limited.

exam_traps.trap: Once a process is outsourced, its risks belong to the supplier.
exam_traps.why: The hiring organization keeps accountability for risks to its objectives. Management must still govern, monitor and control the relationship.

key_terms.definition: An outside person or entity that supplies the organization with products or services, such as a vendor or contractor.
A contract term that lets the organization, or its auditors, examine the third party's records and controls.
The IIA's mandatory baseline for assurance on cybersecurity governance, risk management and controls.

subtopics.name: Culture and Management Reporting Audits
subtopics.definition: Audits of culture and of management reporting are assurance engagements over two things that shape every decision: how people behave and what information leaders receive.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Controls on paper fail when behavior works against them, and boards decide badly on unreliable reports. These engagements look past individual transactions to the conditions around them.
how_it_works: An audit of culture examines whether behavior in the organization supports its objectives and ethical expectations.
It treats behavior like any other risk: are the governance, risk management and control processes over it designed well and working?
Typical subjects are the tone leaders set, incentives, speak-up channels such as hotlines, training, and how misconduct is handled.
Evidence mixes numbers and narrative, for example survey results, complaint and staff turnover data, interviews and observation.
An audit of management reporting examines how management's reports are produced: where the data comes from, how it is compiled and how it is reviewed.
The question is whether decision makers receive accurate, reliable financial and operational information.
subtopics.example: After a mis-selling scandal at a rival, the board of an Australian insurer asks for assurance on sales culture. Mele, an internal auditor, does not rely on the staff survey alone. Mele reviews how bonuses are set, reads complaint and speak-up data, and interviews branch teams about pressure to sell. Mele compares the results with the code of conduct and reports the gaps to the chief audit executive.

review: Compare incentive schemes with the behavior the organization says it expects
Trace a sample of board report figures back to source data
Evaluate how concerns raised by staff are investigated and escalated
evidence: Reconciliations of reported figures to source systems, reperformed by the audit team
Exit interview themes, disciplinary records and hotline case logs
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management align incentives and reporting controls with the behavior and accuracy the board expects.
audit_focus.decides: The board and senior management set expectations for behavior

subtopics.isaca_rule: Culture can be audited: assess the processes that shape behavior, using several kinds of evidence. For management reporting, assess the process behind the numbers, not only one report.

exam_traps.trap: A culture audit is a staff satisfaction survey run by internal audit.
exam_traps.why: A survey is one source of evidence. The engagement assesses governance, risk management and control over behavior, such as tone, incentives and how concerns are handled.

exam_traps.trap: Culture is too soft to give assurance on.
exam_traps.why: Behavior leaves evidence: incentives, complaints, turnover, decisions. The Standards expect the internal audit plan to respond to changes in organizational culture.

key_terms.definition: The shared values and habits that shape how people in an organization act: 'the way we do things'.
The example and messages leaders give about what behavior is expected.
The regular reports, financial and operational, that managers and the board use to run and oversee the organization.

topics.overview: Advisory work takes many forms, from training to advice on a new system. This topic describes the internal auditor's role in each kind the syllabus lists and the line that role must not cross: advise and facilitate, never decide, approve or own.
can_do: Describe the internal auditor's part in each kind of advisory work
Tell advising on a design from approving or owning it
Explain what must happen before assurance is given on an area internal audit advised on
Describe how benchmarking and process mapping help management

subtopics.name: Risk and Control Training and Internal Control Assessments
subtopics.definition: Risk and control training and facilitated control assessments are advisory services in which internal auditors teach and guide while managers assess and own their own controls.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Managers who understand risk and control run better processes between audits. The danger is the auditor ending up as the author of management's assessment, and later auditing their own conclusions.
how_it_works: The Standards list training, and leading discussions on risk and control, among their examples of advisory services.
In training, the internal auditor explains concepts such as risk, control and good practice; management applies them.
In a control self-assessment, managers and staff judge their own risks and controls. It is a first-line activity.
The internal auditor may facilitate the workshop, supply a method, ask probing questions and challenge assumptions.
The ratings, the conclusions and the action plans belong to management, not to the facilitator.
Later assurance may draw on the results, but only after the auditors judge how far that work can be relied on.
subtopics.example: The operations team of a Dutch food distributor asks internal audit to run a workshop on warehouse risks. Sanne, the internal auditor, explains the rating scale, keeps the discussion moving and questions ratings that look optimistic. The warehouse managers set the final ratings and name the action owners. Sanne records in the file that internal audit facilitated and that the assessment is management's own.

review: Inspect session records for who made each scoring decision
Compare training content with the risks the trained teams actually face
evidence: Attendance lists and scored worksheets signed by the participating managers
Engagement terms describing internal audit's part in the sessions
audit_focus.recommend: Have line management sign the self-assessment results and track the resulting actions to completion.
audit_focus.decides: Line managers decide the scores and the follow-up

subtopics.isaca_rule: Teach and facilitate; do not assess for them. In training and control self-assessment the internal auditor brings method and challenge, while management owns the ratings, the conclusions and the actions.

exam_traps.trap: Because internal audit ran the workshop, the control self-assessment results are internal audit's assurance.
exam_traps.why: Facilitating is advisory work and gives no assurance. The assessment is management's own, and any later assurance needs the auditors' own evaluation.

exam_traps.trap: Training managers on controls impairs independence, so auditors should decline.
exam_traps.why: Training is a recognized advisory service. Objectivity is kept by not taking on management responsibility, not by refusing to share knowledge.

key_terms.definition: A process in which managers and staff evaluate the risks and controls in their own area.
The person who guides a session and its method without owning its conclusions.
Work done by operational management, which owns and manages risk day to day.

subtopics.name: Advising on System Design, Due Diligence and Data Privacy
subtopics.definition: Advising on system design, due diligence and data privacy means giving management risk and control input on a new system, a planned deal or personal data handling.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Building a control in is cheaper than adding it later, and a bad deal or privacy breach is hard to undo. Early advice is valuable as long as decisions stay with management.
how_it_works: System design and development: the auditor advises on risks and controls while a system is designed and built.
The auditor may sit on a project committee as an adviser, but should not take part in its decisions.
The auditor does not design, approve, sign off or implement the system or its controls.
Due diligence: before a major deal or new third-party relationship, the auditor may advise on the target's risks and controls. Management decides whether to proceed.
Data privacy: the auditor advises on privacy risks and whether planned controls meet laws and policies. A manager owns the privacy program.
If assurance on the same area follows, the chief audit executive must confirm objectivity is not impaired and assign staff to manage it.
subtopics.example: A Saudi retailer is building a loyalty app that stores customers' personal data. Reem, an internal auditor, joins the project steering committee as a non-voting adviser. Reem points out that the design lacks consent records and access logging, and suggests options. When the project manager asks Reem to approve the final design, Reem declines, explains that approval is management's, and documents the advice given.

review: Inspect project minutes for any vote or approval by an internal auditor
Compare the advice given with the scope agreed for the advisory engagement
evidence: Committee terms of reference listing members with and without a vote
Written memo of suggestions sent to the sponsor, with the reply
audit_focus.recommend: Have the project sponsor sign the design and record how internal audit's suggestions were handled.
audit_focus.decides: Management approves the design and decides whether a deal proceeds

subtopics.isaca_rule: Advise early, decide never. The internal auditor gives input on risks and controls; management designs, approves and owns. Later assurance on that area needs the chief audit executive's confirmation that objectivity is intact.

exam_traps.trap: Signing off the controls in a new system is the most useful help internal audit can give.
exam_traps.why: Sign-off is a management decision. An auditor who approves the design has taken management responsibility and cannot later assess it objectively.

exam_traps.trap: As a steering committee member, the internal auditor should vote like everyone else.
exam_traps.why: The auditor contributes questions and insight as an adviser. Taking part in decisions would put the auditor in management's seat.

key_terms.definition: A careful investigation of a company, partner or supplier before entering a deal or relationship.
The risk of bias when someone later assesses work they designed, decided or performed.

subtopics.name: Benchmarking and Process Mapping
subtopics.definition: Benchmarking and process mapping are advisory tools: one compares an activity with others to find better practice, the other draws how a process flows from start to finish.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Managers often cannot see their own process whole or know how peers perform. A comparison or a map gives them a factual base for improvement decisions that remain theirs.
how_it_works: Internal benchmarking compares the same measure across different areas of the organization.
External benchmarking compares the organization's information with that of similar organizations.
The auditor gathers comparable data, explains the differences and points to practices worth considering. Management decides what to change.
A process map, flowchart or narrative shows each step, who performs it, and where decisions and handoffs occur.
Mapping reveals where risks arise and where controls sit, are missing or are duplicated.
The same tools serve assurance work too: benchmarks can be criteria, and maps help auditors understand an activity.
subtopics.example: The head of customer service at an Indian telecom asks why complaints take so long to close. Arjun, an internal auditor, maps the complaint process with the team and finds three handoffs with no owner. Arjun also compares closing times across the company's four regional centers and shares what the fastest center does differently. Arjun presents the map and the comparison and leaves the choice of changes to the head of customer service.

review: Walk the mapped process with the people who perform each step
Compare like with like before drawing conclusions from benchmark data
evidence: Flowchart signed as accurate by the manager accountable for it
Benchmark data with its source and the period covered
audit_focus.recommend: Have the accountable manager assign each unowned step and select which comparison findings to act on.
audit_focus.decides: The manager accountable for the process, not internal audit

subtopics.isaca_rule: Benchmarking and mapping give management facts, not instructions. The internal auditor compares, draws and explains; the process owner decides what to change and owns the process afterward.

exam_traps.trap: After mapping the process, internal audit should redesign it and roll out the new version.
exam_traps.why: Redesign and rollout are management's work. The auditor's map and suggestions are advice; owning the change would be a management responsibility.

exam_traps.trap: A benchmark shows what the organization must do.
exam_traps.why: A benchmark is a comparison, not a rule. Differences in size, risk and strategy matter, so management weighs the result before acting.

key_terms.definition: Comparing performance between units or sites inside one organization.
Comparing performance with similar organizations or recognized good practice.
A diagram of a process's steps, people and decision points, from start to finish.
The manager accountable for how a process is designed and performs.

topics.overview: Independence belongs to the internal audit function and comes from where it sits. This topic covers the reporting lines that protect or threaten it, what the board and the chief audit executive each do to guard it, and what happens when budgets, scope or access are restricted. It is also a CIA Challenge Exam topic.
can_do: Identify reporting arrangements that impair the function's independence
Describe what the board does to protect independence
Describe what the chief audit executive must confirm, disclose and document
Identify the right response to a budget cut, a scope limitation or restricted access

subtopics.name: Independence and the Reporting Lines
subtopics.definition: Independence is the internal audit function's freedom from conditions that could keep it from doing its work without bias; it rests on a direct reporting line to the board.
subtopics.why_it_matters: If the people being audited control the auditors' boss, pay or access, findings can be softened or buried. A direct line to the board lets internal audit report without interference.
how_it_works: The chief audit executive reports directly to the board. The Standards also call this functional reporting.
For day-to-day administration, the chief audit executive often reports to a member of management: the administrative line.
Reporting administratively to the chief executive officer is a leading practice. Another senior officer may work with safeguards.
Independence may be impaired when the chief audit executive lacks direct communication with the board.
Another threat: assurance over an area run by the senior officer who is the chief audit executive's administrative boss, such as treasury under the chief financial officer.

rows.label: Reports to
cells: A member of management, ideally the chief executive officer

rows.label: Typical matters
cells: Charter, plan, budget approval, results, appointment and removal
Day-to-day matters such as expenses and human resources administration

rows.label: Why it exists
cells: Lets the function work and report without interference
Gives access to senior management and the standing to challenge it

rows.label: Main threat
cells: Missing or weak: independence is not supported
Auditing areas run by the administrative boss

subtopics.example: At a Turkish construction group, the chief audit executive reports only to the chief financial officer and meets the audit committee once a year with the chief financial officer present. Elif, an internal auditor assigned to audit treasury, sees that treasury also reports to the chief financial officer. Elif raises the concern with the chief audit executive, who discloses the impairment to the board and proposes safeguards.

review: Compare the actual reporting lines with those documented in the charter
Identify engagements covering areas run by the administrative reporting officer
evidence: Calendar invitations and minutes of meetings held with board members
Organization chart and charter showing both reporting lines
audit_focus.recommend: Have the board arrange outside oversight for engagements in areas under the officer who handles internal audit's administration.
audit_focus.decides: The board determines the function's reporting relationships and positioning

subtopics.isaca_rule: Functional reporting to the board makes the function independent. An administrative line to management is normal, ideally to the chief executive officer. It becomes a threat when it blocks access to the board or when internal audit audits its administrative boss's own areas.

exam_traps.trap: Reporting administratively to the chief financial officer always breaches the Standards.
exam_traps.why: The Standards call chief executive officer reporting a leading practice and allow another senior officer with safeguards. The threat is assurance over that officer's own areas, or lost access to the board.

exam_traps.trap: An auditor with a personal conflict has an independence problem.
exam_traps.why: That is an objectivity impairment of the person, disclosed to the chief audit executive or a supervisor. Independence concerns the function's position and goes to the board.

key_terms.definition: The function's freedom, gained from its position, to plan, perform and report its work without being steered by those it audits.
Each internal auditor's unbiased state of mind when judging evidence and reaching conclusions.

subtopics.name: How the Board Protects Independence
subtopics.definition: Board protection of independence is the set of board actions, listed as essential conditions, that place the internal audit function beyond management's control.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The chief audit executive cannot protect independence alone, because the pressure usually comes from people more senior. Only the board has the authority to stand behind the function.
how_it_works: The board creates a direct line between itself and the chief audit executive and the function.
The board authorizes the appointment and removal of the chief audit executive. Senior management gives input.
On the chief audit executive's performance evaluation and pay, the board gives input to senior management. The Standards do not say the board sets them.
The board meets the chief audit executive without senior management present: at least yearly as a consideration, quarterly as a leading practice.
The board requires positioning free of management interference and asks whether scope, access, authority or resources are being restricted.
subtopics.example: The chief executive officer of a Colombian utility wants to dismiss the chief audit executive after a critical report on a major contract. Colleagues ask Valentina, a senior internal auditor, whether that can happen. Valentina explains that removal needs the board's authorization, and that the chief audit executive can raise the matter in a private session with the audit committee.

review: Inspect minutes for the resolution that hired or dismissed the chief audit executive
Confirm closed meetings with no executives present actually took place
evidence: Attendance records of closed meetings, showing who was in the room
Human resources file showing who contributed to the appraisal and salary review
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive discuss any missing board protection with the board and document the outcome.
audit_focus.decides: The board holds the hiring and dismissal decision

subtopics.isaca_rule: The board protects independence by holding the key levers: the direct reporting line, appointment and removal of the chief audit executive, private sessions, and inquiries about restrictions. On pay and evaluation the board gives input; it does not set them.

exam_traps.trap: The board sets the chief audit executive's pay.
exam_traps.why: The essential condition is that the board gives input to senior management on performance evaluation and remuneration. Appointment and removal are what the board authorizes.

exam_traps.trap: Senior management may remove the chief audit executive if the board is told afterward.
exam_traps.why: The board authorizes removal; senior management only provides input. A chief audit executive who could be dismissed by management alone would not be independent of it.

key_terms.definition: A meeting of the board and the chief audit executive with no senior management in the room.
The board's decision power over who becomes, and who stops being, chief audit executive.
Acts that hinder the function, such as withholding information or restricting access to people, records or property.

subtopics.name: The Chief Audit Executive's Duties to Confirm, Disclose and Safeguard
subtopics.definition: The chief audit executive's independence duties are to confirm the function's independence to the board at least yearly and to disclose and manage anything that impairs it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Boards cannot protect what they are not told about. A yearly confirmation plus prompt disclosure of incidents lets the board act before an impairment damages the credibility of internal audit's results.
how_it_works: At least once a year, the chief audit executive must confirm the function's organizational independence to the board.
The confirmation also covers any incident that may have impaired independence, and what was done about it.
Current or proposed roles that could impair independence, in fact or appearance, must be discussed with the board and senior management, with advice on safeguards.
Ongoing role beyond internal auditing: the charter documents the responsibilities, nature of work and safeguards, and assurance over that area comes from another source.
Temporary role: an independent third party gives assurance during the assignment and for 12 months after, and there is a plan to hand the role back to management.
If the governing structure does not support independence, the chief audit executive documents what limits it and any safeguards.
subtopics.example: Hamid, chief audit executive of a Moroccan port operator, is asked to run the compliance unit for six months after its head resigns. Hamid discusses the impairment with the board and senior management, agrees that an outside firm will give assurance over compliance during the assignment and for 12 months afterward, and sets a date to hand the unit back. Hamid reports this in the yearly independence confirmation.

review: Inspect the latest independence statement given to the board and its list of incidents
Trace each nonaudit role to charter wording, safeguards and outside assurance
evidence: Contract with the external firm covering areas internal audit cannot review
Minutes in which directors received the statement and discussed incidents
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive keep a log of incidents and nonaudit duties and present it at each board meeting.
audit_focus.decides: The board agrees to each extra duty and its protections

subtopics.isaca_rule: The chief audit executive confirms independence to the board at least yearly and tells the board about impairments, actual or perceived. A role beyond internal auditing needs safeguards: outside assurance over that area and, for a temporary role, 12 more months of it plus a plan to hand back.

exam_traps.trap: An independence impairment is disclosed to senior management, who decide whether the board needs to know.
exam_traps.why: The confirmation and the incidents go to the board, and they cover impairments in fact or in appearance. Management does not filter the message.

key_terms.definition: A measure that manages an impairment, such as outside assurance, disclosure or reassignment.
A responsibility the chief audit executive holds beyond internal auditing, such as compliance or risk management.

subtopics.name: Budget Limits, Scope Limitations and Restricted Access
subtopics.definition: Budget limits, scope limitations and restricted access are constraints that stop internal audit from doing the work its charter and plan call for.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Nobody needs to forbid an audit to stop it. Starving the budget, narrowing the scope or withholding records does the same more quietly, so the Standards send these matters to the board.
how_it_works: Cutting the budget so far that the function cannot do what its charter requires may impair independence.
The chief audit executive seeks budget approval from the board and promptly tells the board and senior management the impact of insufficient resources, with a strategy to obtain them.
