A scope limitation is an assurance engagement condition, such as a resource constraint or restricted access, that prevents work the program expected.
Internal auditors discuss a scope limitation with management when it is identified, aiming to resolve it. If that fails, the chief audit executive elevates it to the board.
A scope limitation is explained in the final communication of the assurance engagement.
subtopics.example: During a payroll audit at an Irish hospital trust, the human resources director refuses Siobhan, the internal auditor, access to executive pay records, calling them confidential. Siobhan discusses the restriction with the director, citing the charter, but it is not lifted. Siobhan documents the scope limitation and reports it to the chief audit executive, who elevates it to the board.

review: Compare approved budget and staffing with what the plan requires
Trace each scope limitation from discovery to resolution or escalation
Confirm scope limitations appear in the final communication
evidence: Workpaper notes of who refused what, when, and the reply given
Board minutes showing the matter was raised and what directors asked
Gap analysis of hours needed against hours funded
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management lift restrictions on records and staff, or explain them to the board in writing.
audit_focus.decides: The board decides whether to intervene with senior management

subtopics.isaca_rule: Limits on budget, scope or access are independence matters. Try to resolve a scope limitation with management first. If it stays unresolved, the chief audit executive takes it to the board, and the final communication explains it.

exam_traps.trap: Settle a scope limitation quietly with the manager and leave it out of the report.
exam_traps.why: Discussion with management comes first, but the chief audit executive elevates an unresolved limitation to the board, and the final communication explains scope limitations.

exam_traps.trap: A budget cut is an administrative matter for the finance department, not an independence issue.
exam_traps.why: A cut that stops the function meeting its charter responsibilities is an undue limitation. The chief audit executive reports its impact to the board, which approves the budget.

key_terms.definition: A condition in an assurance engagement that prevents the auditors from doing the work the program expected.
A restriction, such as an inadequate budget, that keeps the function from operating effectively.

subtopics.memory_aid: Discuss with management, elevate to the board, explain in the report.

topics.topic_name: Internal audit and the Three Lines Model
topics.overview: The Three Lines Model explains who does what in governance: the board oversees, management owns and manages risk in first-line and second-line roles, and internal audit gives independent assurance as the third line. The model comes from The IIA's 2026 Statement of Position, not from the Standards. It is also a CIA Challenge Exam topic.
can_do: Recognize who sits in each line and what the board and senior management do
Tell second-line roles, which are part of management, from the third line's independent assurance
Recognize first-line and second-line duties that would impair internal audit's independence
Name the safeguards needed when internal audit or its head takes on another role

subtopics.name: The Three Lines Model and Its Roles
subtopics.definition: The Three Lines Model is The IIA's description of how the board, management and internal audit each contribute assurance and advice so the organization is well governed.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Clear roles prevent gaps where nobody checks a risk and overlaps where the checker is also the doer. Exam questions ask you to place a task with the right party.
how_it_works: The board gives direction and oversight, sets risk appetite and expectations, and delegates authority and resources to management.
Senior management designs the structures and processes to achieve objectives and answers to the board for managing risk.
First line: operational management owns risk day to day and designs, implements and operates processes and controls.
Second line: specialist roles such as risk management and compliance give expert support, advice, monitoring and challenge to the first line.
Third line: the internal audit function gives independent, objective assurance and advice, including over the second line, and reports functionally to the board.
External auditors and regulators serve outside parties and are not among the three lines.
subtopics.example: A fintech in Estonia hires its first risk manager and asks internal audit who now does what. Kristjan, an internal auditor, sets it out: product teams own and control their risks, the risk manager supports and challenges them, and internal audit independently assesses both and reports to the board. Kristjan adds the three roles to the planning notes for the next engagement.

review: Compare documented roles for each line with what people actually do
Identify risks that no line monitors or that two lines duplicate
evidence: Assurance map showing who covers each significant risk
Job descriptions and committee charters for the risk and compliance teams
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management document which role owns, monitors and independently assesses each significant risk.
audit_focus.decides: The board and senior management define roles and responsibilities

subtopics.isaca_rule: Management owns and manages risk, in first-line and second-line roles. Internal audit, the third line, gives independent assurance and advice and reports functionally to the board. External auditors and regulators sit outside the three lines.

exam_traps.trap: The second line is independent in the same way internal audit is.
exam_traps.why: Second-line roles are part of management and usually report through it. Only the third line reports functionally to the board.

exam_traps.trap: The external auditor is the fourth line of the model.
exam_traps.why: The Statement of Position treats external auditors and regulators as other providers outside the three lines. They serve external stakeholders.

key_terms.definition: Operational management, front and back office, which owns and manages risk and runs the controls.
Management's specialist risk roles, such as risk management and compliance, that support, monitor and challenge the first line.
The internal audit function: independent assurance and advice, with functional reporting to the board.

subtopics.memory_aid: First line owns, second line supports and challenges, third line assures.

subtopics.name: Independence Across the Lines and Coordination
subtopics.definition: Independence across the lines differs by design: the first line is not independent, the second is part of management, and only the third reports functionally to the board.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A board that treats every source of comfort as equally independent will over-trust management's own checks. Knowing the differences shows why internal audit must also give assurance over the second line.
how_it_works: First line: not independent by design, because it is directly responsible for the processes and controls.
Second line: more objective than the first because it is separate from operations, but it is part of management and reports to senior management or a board-level committee.
Third line: the highest organizational independence. Its authority is set by the board or by law, and it can report without undue influence from management.
Coordination and reliance reduce duplication and gaps. An assurance map shows who covers which risk.
Internal audit can integrate assurance and may decline to rely on work of poor quality. Outsourcing an activity does not change its line.

rows.label: Who
cells: Specialist functions such as risk and compliance

rows.label: Main job
cells: Owns risk; designs and runs controls

rows.label: Reports to
cells: Senior management or a board-level committee

rows.label: Independence
cells: Part of management; some separation from operations

rows.label: Typical limit
cells: May overlook or rationalize weak controls
May be impaired by reporting through management
Periodic, risk-based coverage; less operational exposure

subtopics.example: The compliance team of a Hong Kong brokerage reports that all trading controls passed its monitoring. The audit committee asks whether an internal audit is still needed. Mei, an internal auditor, explains that compliance is a second-line role inside management, so its monitoring is useful but is not independent assurance. Mei proposes that internal audit review the monitoring's quality and rely on it where it holds up.

review: Evaluate the competence, objectivity and methods of second-line monitoring before relying on it
Compare second-line results with the internal auditors' own sample tests
evidence: Reperformed sample of the second line's monitoring tests
Written rationale for using, or not using, another team's test results
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive document the basis for any reliance on second-line work and report gaps to the board.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive chooses whether to rely; the board keeps sight of it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Independence is highest in the third line. Second-line monitoring is management's own work, so internal audit gives assurance over it and relies on it only after evaluating it. The chief audit executive remains responsible for internal audit's conclusions.

exam_traps.trap: If risk management and compliance already checked an area, internal audit should leave it alone.
exam_traps.why: Coordination avoids waste, but the third line also gives assurance over the second line. Reliance is a choice made after evaluating that work.

exam_traps.trap: Outsourcing internal audit or a compliance task makes it independent.
exam_traps.why: Outsourcing does not change which line an activity belongs to or the board's accountability. A provider is classed by the function that engages and directs its work.

key_terms.definition: A matrix of significant risks and the internal and external providers that give assurance over each.
Using another provider's work in place of doing it again, on a documented basis.

subtopics.name: First-Line and Second-Line Duties That Impair Independence
subtopics.definition: Impairing duties are first-line or second-line responsibilities, such as deciding risk responses, owning policies or running controls, that internal audit cannot hold and still assess objectively.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An auditor who decides how a risk is treated will later be asked whether that decision was sound. Nobody assesses their own work objectively, so deciding and assuring are kept apart.
how_it_works: Internal audit must not determine, prioritize, select, implement or own risk responses. Those are management decisions.
It must not own management's follow-up of actions or the organization's reporting to external parties.
It should not own final policies, or run a continuing risk assessment process and then audit that same process.
The board sets risk appetite. Internal audit gives assurance on whether it is established and built into decisions.
Still allowed as advice: suggesting methods, facilitating risk workshops and training, challenging assumptions and sharing good practice.
Still allowed for its own work: assessing risks to rank engagements, keeping the audit universe, and consolidating assurance results.
subtopics.example: At a Peruvian mining company, the chief operating officer asks internal audit to keep the corporate risk register and choose the treatment for each risk, since the auditors 'know risk best'. Rosa, an internal auditor, explains that deciding how each risk is treated is management's responsibility. Rosa offers to facilitate a risk workshop instead and refers the request to the chief audit executive.

review: Inspect the charter and job descriptions for management duties held by internal auditors
Identify treatment plans or policy documents that an internal auditor signed
evidence: Risk committee minutes naming the person who approved each treatment
Charter section describing internal audit's role in risk management
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management name a first-line or second-line manager as accountable for each treatment plan, policy and action tracker.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides risk responses and is accountable to the board

subtopics.isaca_rule: Internal audit may advise, facilitate and challenge. It must not decide, select, implement or own risk responses, and it does not set risk appetite. A task that makes internal audit the owner of what it later assesses belongs to management.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit knows the risks best, so it should choose the risk responses.
exam_traps.why: Choosing and implementing responses is management decision-making. Internal audit gives assurance on whether responses are adequate and may advise on options.

exam_traps.trap: Facilitating a risk workshop is a second-line duty internal audit must refuse.
exam_traps.why: Facilitation, training and challenge are advisory services internal audit may provide, as long as management owns the outputs and decisions.

key_terms.definition: What management decides to do about a risk.
How much risk, and of what kinds, the organization is prepared to take on to reach its goals; set by the board.
Internal audit's list of the units, processes and systems that could be audited.

subtopics.name: Safeguards When Internal Audit Takes On Other Roles
subtopics.definition: Safeguards are the measures that keep assurance credible when internal audit, or the chief audit executive, performs or appears to perform first-line or second-line work.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Small organizations and urgent situations sometimes leave no one else to do the job. This is allowed only with transparency, board approval and independent assurance over the affected area.
how_it_works: Discuss the role with the board and senior management, and advise them on safeguards for actual, potential or perceived impairments.
For an ongoing role, document the responsibilities, the nature of the work and the safeguards in the charter. The board approves the wider remit.
Obtain assurance over that area from an independent party. Internal audit cannot give assurance over its own second-line work.
For a temporary role, outside assurance continues for 12 months after it ends, and a plan returns the work to management.
Assurance engagements over any function the chief audit executive is responsible for are overseen by an independent party outside internal audit.
subtopics.example: A small Icelandic pension fund has no compliance officer, so the board asks Sigrun, the chief audit executive, to run compliance monitoring permanently. Sigrun explains the self-review threat, and the board approves the role with safeguards: the charter describes the duties, an outside firm audits compliance and reports to the board, and the arrangement is re-evaluated yearly. Sigrun confirms the safeguards in the next independence report.

review: Compare duties held outside auditing with what the charter says about them
Confirm someone independent reviewed every area that internal audit itself runs
evidence: External reviewer's report on those areas, addressed to the directors
Resolution in which directors accepted the added duties and their risks
Dated handover schedule for any duty held only for a time
audit_focus.recommend: Have the board commission an external review of any area where internal audit performs management duties.
audit_focus.decides: The board accepts the added duty and acknowledges the impairment

subtopics.isaca_rule: A safeguard never lets internal audit audit itself. For a first-line or second-line duty: disclose it to the board, write it into the charter, and get assurance from an independent party, continuing for 12 months after a temporary duty is handed back.

exam_traps.trap: With good safeguards, internal audit can give assurance over the compliance work it performs.
exam_traps.why: The safeguard is that an independent party assures that area or oversees the engagement. Self-review is the threat safeguards exist to remove.

exam_traps.trap: Once a temporary role is handed back, internal audit can audit the area the next month.
exam_traps.why: Independent assurance continues for 12 months after the assignment, and the chief audit executive should discuss with the board whether that is long enough.

key_terms.definition: A competent, objective provider outside the affected area that gives assurance and reports to the board.
A situation that looks like it compromises independence or objectivity, even if it does not in fact.

key_terminologies.Purpose of Internal Auditing: Domain I of the Standards: why internal auditing exists and the conditions under which it works best.
key_terminologies.Global Internal Audit Standards: The IIA's standards for the profession, published in 2024: five domains, 15 principles and 52 standards.
key_terminologies.Requirement: A 'must' in the Standards. It is mandatory.
key_terminologies.Consideration for Implementation: A 'should' or 'may' in the Standards: preferred or optional practice, not mandatory.
key_terminologies.Internal audit function: The person or team that delivers internal audit services in an organization.
key_terminologies.Chief audit executive: The head of internal audit, whatever the job title, who answers for the function's work and its conformance with the Standards.
key_terminologies.Board: The top governing body, for example a board of directors or an audit committee acting for it.
key_terminologies.Senior management: The top executives, usually including the chief executive officer, who answer to the board for carrying out its strategy.
key_terminologies.Internal audit mandate: What the function may do, the part it plays and what it must deliver; set by the board, by law, or both.
key_terminologies.Internal audit charter: The board-approved paper that sets out what internal audit is for, what it may do, where it sits and to whom it reports.
key_terminologies.Essential conditions: Board and senior management activities that Domain III lists as necessary for internal audit to be effective. They are not requirements on the board.
key_terminologies.Assurance services: Engagements where internal auditors test an activity against criteria and state a conclusion others can rely on.
key_terminologies.Advisory services: Advice-only work, such as training or input on a new design. The auditor gives no assurance and makes no management decision.
key_terminologies.Limited and reasonable assurance: Two levels of assurance named in the Standards. The level depends on the kind, timing and amount of work done.
key_terminologies.Criteria: The yardstick for an engagement: what the activity should look like.
key_terminologies.Scope limitation: A condition in an assurance engagement, such as restricted access, that prevents the planned work.
key_terminologies.Independence: The function's freedom, gained from its position, to do and report its work without being steered by those it audits.
key_terminologies.Objectivity: Each internal auditor's unbiased state of mind when judging evidence and reaching conclusions.
key_terminologies.Functional reporting: The chief audit executive's direct reporting line to the board.
key_terminologies.Administrative reporting: The chief audit executive's day-to-day line to a member of management, ideally the chief executive officer.
key_terminologies.Impairment: A condition that weakens independence or objectivity, in fact or in appearance.
key_terminologies.Safeguard: A measure that manages an impairment, such as outside assurance, disclosure or reassignment.
key_terminologies.Three Lines Model: The IIA's model of who owns risk (first line), who supports and challenges (second line) and who gives independent assurance (third line).
key_terminologies.First line: Operational management, which owns and manages risk and runs the controls.
key_terminologies.Second line: Management's specialist roles, such as risk management and compliance, that support, monitor and challenge the first line.
key_terminologies.Third line: The internal audit function, which gives independent assurance and advice and reports functionally to the board.
key_terminologies.Topical Requirement: A mandatory baseline for assurance engagements on a named subject, such as cybersecurity; recommended for advisory work.
key_terminologies.Right-to-audit clause: A contract term that lets the organization or its auditors examine a third party's records and controls.
key_terminologies.Control self-assessment: Managers and staff evaluating the risks and controls in their own area, sometimes with an internal auditor facilitating.
